content:
Hi!

I have just submitted a pull request (lean4#14420) and I wanted to have your feedback.

In this PR, I refactored a bit the proof of excluded-middle (Diaconescu's theorem) and removed the usage of funext, following a trick that I discovered on this MO question by Jean Abou Samra.

The idea is to encode the two functions used in Diaconescu's theorem using another structure (which is just a tuple), for which equality does not require function extensionality.

As a result, we have (run online):

Before

#print axioms em
'Classical.em' depends on axioms: [propext, choice, Quot.sound]

After

#print axioms em
'Classical.em' depends on axioms: [propext, choice]

What do you think of that change? In particular, I was wondering if it was common practice to test for the axiom dependencies in Lean codebase? (I have seen that we have some outputs tested here and there)
I don't want to discourage you, but upstream has rejected previous attempts at changing Classical.em's proof: lean4#2625 lean4#13826

Mauricio Collares said :

I don't want to discourage you, but upstream has rejected previous attempts at changing Classical.em's proof: lean4#2625 lean4#13826

Interesting! Although the change I propose is different from these at it preserves the exact same proof (as would be expressed in natural language), while also making it simpler.

The general policy of both lean4 and mathlib are that they are not interested in reducing axioms employed in a proof; however, since your proof is simpler than the original I think it's still good to have and I would maybe highlight that point more in your PR title/body

IMO the split in lean#13826 is even simpler, as it illuminates exactly where and why propext is used (for p ↔ (p = True)), and seems to show that Diaconescu's theorem is actually about decidable equality. (although I dislike the proof of em_eq there)
In the above, propext is used inside simp, and I still find the proof to be unexplained magic.

Keep in mind that the Lean standard library is the Lean standard library, not a showcase of basic theorems in logic. Proofs being simple and understandable is only relevant in the sense that simple and understandable proofs are often maintainable, but it's fair to say that our proof of Diaconescu's theorem hasn't been a maintenance burden in the past. I think it's great and instructive to discuss and contrast different proofs of the theorem, but the Lean standard library is not the right context to have this discussion in.
